title: Pine tar bar soap
subtitle: A dark, traditional bar for dry or troubled skin
excerpt: Cold-process bar soap with a 15% pine tar inclusion on a coconut and olive base. Pine tar has been used in soap for scalp and skin conditions for well over a century. The bar is dark brown, strong-smelling, and conditioning. Yields seven bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972), medicated soap formulations and pine tar history. Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), pine tar soap ratios; notes that pine tar adds a small amount of saponifiable material and should be treated as part of the oil weight for lye calculations. Soap-Calc (accessed 2026): pine tar SAP value approximately 0.130. Piney tar bars traditionally used at 10-20% pine tar; 15% is the recommended middle point for home use.

recipe.batchNotes: Pine tar is sticky and viscous. Warm it gently to 38°C before incorporating, it won't blend smoothly if cold. Include its weight in the oil total for lye calculation.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pine tar bars cure slowly and benefit from a full 6-week cure. They keep for 2 years.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 2 years in a cool, dry place. The pine tar darkens further as the bar hardens but stabilises. Discard if the bar develops a sharp rancid smell distinct from the normal piney scent, or if orange spots appear.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide that produces soap. Pine tar contributes a small amount of saponifiable material, so its weight is included in the total oil weight for lye calculation.
The point at which the blended soap batter thickens enough to hold a faint trail, the signal that emulsification is underway and the batter is ready to mould.
The percentage of oil left unsaponified in the finished bar, contributing conditioning properties. This recipe uses 5%.

content.text: Pine tar soap is a dark brown, strongly scented cold-process bar with a traditional reputation for dry, itchy, or troubled scalp and skin. The pine tar, a thick, viscous resin distilled from pine wood, gives the bar its characteristic brown colour, smoky-piney smell, and conditioning quality. At 15% of the oil weight on a coconut and olive base, it balances the cleaning power of coconut with the moisturising quality of olive. Seven bars; the full 6-week cure is recommended.

content.text: Put on protective gloves and goggles. Work in a well-ventilated space, pine tar has a strong smell and the lye fumes both need moving air. Pour the sodium hydroxide slowly into the distilled water in the HDPE pitcher, stirring until dissolved. Cool to 38-42°C.

Warm the pine tar gently to around 38°C so it pours easily. Melt the coconut oil, then combine with the olive oil and the warmed pine tar. The mixed oils will be a dark amber colour. Bring to 38-42°C.

Pour into the mould, smooth the top, and insulate with a towel. Leave 24-48 hours. The batter will be dark throughout, there is no visual gel-phase transition to see, but the
Unmould when firm. The bar will be very dark. Cut into 7 bars wearing gloves, fresh soap is still caustic. Cure on a ventilated rack for 4-6 weeks, turning every 2 weeks.
Store cured bars on a ventilated rack in a cool, dry cupboard. The

oils condition the skin throughout the bar's 2-year shelf life. The piney scent is strongest on fresh bars and matures over the cure. Discard if the bar develops a sharp, rancid smell clearly different from the normal pine-resin scent, or if orange spots appear on the cut face.
